Every year, on the first morning, somebody comes to me and says the same thing. My English is fine until I need one specific word, and then it disappears, and I stop. Here is what I tell them. Native speakers lose words too. It happens to me three or four times a day. The difference is that we do not stop. We describe the thing. It is the person who signs the contracts. It is the report that shows the numbers every month. It is the place where the money comes in. Nobody in that room is waiting for the perfect word. They are waiting for the idea. So when the word goes, do not go silent and do not apologize. Say hold on, describe it, and keep moving.

On my first day in the program, I tried to explain our credit process and I got stuck on one word. I knew it in my own language. I knew it was there. And I stood there for maybe ten seconds, which feels like ten minutes. That night I wrote four sentences on a small card and put it in my pocket. Hold on. It is sort of like. It is the thing that. What I mean is. The next day the word disappeared again, in the middle of a case. I took a breath, said it is the money that the client cannot pay back, and the professor said, right, the default rate, and wrote it on the board. Nobody remembered that I forgot the word. They remembered the point.
